They are in the Kingdom Animalia in the clade Deuterostomia, Phylum Chordata, Subphylum Vertebrata within the Reptile Class. This bird is identified as a Verterbate due to the fact that it can walk on two legs and support its head with a neck and shoulders, thus having an endoskeleton and internal organs. description:
White Rock lake, Sunset Bay
Photo 1:
American Black Duck &  Her Mallard Mate
2017 winter a female American black duck visited White Rock lake & caused much excitement in the birder world.  She stayed a couple of weeks with her mallard mate, then traveled on. In 2018 winter she returned.  Again with her mallard mate.  All the birders who missed her the prior winter turned up in hopes of adding her species to their life list. I had captured her the first winter but was happy to see her again this time.  On a cold morning, she & her mate were puffed up trying to stay warm.  So far this is my only shot that captured both birds.
Photo 2:
Sleeping in the Sunshine
While her mate went swimming, the black duck settled in for a nap.  Now you can see the little patch of blue peeking out from some wing feathers. American black ducks have a blue speculum surrounded by dark wing feathers that identify them.  Mallards have their's outlined in white.
Photo 3:
Chocolate
She is beautiful, her color looks like rich delicious Belgium chocolate.  That is her mate in the water behind her.  
Photo 4:
Showing Off That Beautiful Speculum
This was the last shot I took of her.  I hope she continues to show up each winter.

description:
Mallards can be better described as ducks or for their scientific name Anas Platyrhynchos who reside in habitats of basically any wet land habitats varying from areas pertaining to marshes, rivers, city parks and even estuaries all according to The Cornell lab of ornithology’s article on All About Birds: Mallard Life History. Their physical appearance that can help define that can differ depending on if the species happens to be male or female, thus being that for male mallards they exhibit rounds heads that often are a deep green in color in comparison the rest of their bodies which are brown. Just like the Mallard presented in the photo captured with a female mallard trailing shortly behind. They also obtain a flat, wide type bill and round bodies that often times can be a distinct shape if seen floating on top of a body of water. Whereas for females they are slightly different in their appearance, such as unlike the male species their whole body is brown with exception of their beaks that can also sometimes be orange or brown. Although, the one characteristic they share is their web feet feature used to help them maneuver throughout the water (Ornithology). Mallards can be classified as a type of deuterostome due to its mammal/ amphibian features and them being able to reproduce sexually as well. With that being said their taxonomic group classifies them as belonging to the animalia kingdom, Aves class, Anseriformes order, Anatidae family, the Anatinae genus, and like mentioned before the Anas platyrhynchos Linnaeus species. (Peterson, 2009). Not to mention that as far as ecologically this species tends to reside in the upper Northern Hemisphere, stated within a report Mallard Duck Information.

These birds are adapted for swimming, floating on the water surface, and in some cases diving in at least shallow water. The family contains around 146 species in 43 genera. (The magpie goose is no longer considered to be part of the Anatidae and is now placed in its own family, Anseranatidae.)

They are generally herbivorous, and are monogamous breeders. A number of species undertake annual migrations. A few species have been domesticated for agriculture, and many others are hunted for food and recreation. Five species have become extinct since 1600, and many more are threatened with extinction.

Description and ecology
The ducks, geese, and swans are small- to large-sized birds with a broad and elongated general body plan.[2] Diving species vary from this in being rounder. Extant species range in size from the cotton pygmy goose, at as little as 26.5 cm (10.5 in) and 164 g (5.8 oz), to the trumpeter swan, at as much as 183 cm (6 ft) and 17.2 kg (38 lb). The wings are short and pointed, and supported by strong wing muscles that generate rapid beats in flight. They typically have long necks, although this varies in degree between species. The legs are short, strong, and set far to the back of the body (more so in the more aquatic species), and have a leathery feel with a scaly texture. Combined with their body shape, this can make some species awkward on land, but they are stronger walkers than other marine and water birds such as grebes or petrels. They typically have webbed feet, though a few species such as the Nene have secondarily lost their webbing. The bills are made of soft keratin with a thin and sensitive layer of skin on top (which has a leathery feel when touched). For most species, the shape of the bill tends to be more flattened to a greater or lesser extent. These contain serrated lamellae which are particularly well defined in the filter-feeding species.Their feathers are excellent at shedding water due to special oils. They are found generally around ponds and are evenly distributed around the US.

description:
I observed these ducks in the pond at an Equestrian Center. The area the ducks were hanging out in was the shallow water of the pond where there was a lot of grass and plants. They were ducking their heads into the water in order to catch fish and tadpoles to eat. This is called "dabble feeding". Mallards do not dive for their food, so this is how they catch a meal. There were 3 of them together. At the time of the observation, the skies were clear, and it was humid, with the temperature being about 85 degrees F. The ducks had dark and light brown feathers. Two of them had white chests and dark brown beaks. These ducks were females. The other had a black head, yellow beak, and black feathers under his wings near his tail feathers. This one was a male. They were all roughly the same size (about a foot tall).

Unusual Duck
This duck is a bit different.  That elongated body is muscovy and the head and neck mallard.  With some unusual facial markings.  Looks like a mallard x Muscovy hybrid.
Photo 2:
Angel Wing
When the duck turned and came closer, I noticed it had signs of angel wing.  This is a syndrome affecting water birds that eat too much bread.  This  causes a nutritional deficiency in vitamins and minerals combined with a high level of carbohydrates and sugars.  It affects their ability to fly.  If you enjoy feeding ducks, better to bring along some cracked corn or frozen peas.

description:
White Rock lake, Winfrey point
Little Mama
Week 3 for the mallard nest and she looked so sweet sitting there.  Still very hidden.  I was able to find a high spot where I could look down on her without flushing her off the nest.  Don't know how many eggs she ended up with since she never left the nest again while I was there.  This is the last time I saw her.  By the following week there was no more nest.  Grass was mowed and bits of egg shells were there from 2 remaining eggs.  Hopefully she was able to hatch the viable eggs and only the bad ones remained when the area was mowed.  There would have been more egg shell if the entire batch was still there at time of mowing.

description:
In these two photos, we have two male and two female Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos). These water foul hang out at the pond on Slippery Rock campus in front of Keister road. Earlier in the season, two families of Canada Goose (Branta canadensis) lived in this pond. But since they migrated for the winter, the Mallards have the pond to themselves. 

The Mallard is a dabbler, meaning they find their food by flipping upside down with their head and neck submerged underwater.
 The male Mallard has a shiny green head with a white ring around the base of the neck and a yellow bill. Their chest is dark brown, their wings are a lighter shade of brown, and their tails are white.
The female Mallard is different shades of brown. Her bill is light orange with a strap of brown around the middle. She has orange legs and a purple wing patch bordered with white that is revealed when she is in flight.
The average length of a Mallard is 24". They live in ponds, rivers, marshes, and marinas. 

The weather for this day was a high of 50 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of 32 degrees Fahrenheit.  Layer in the day, we had .19 inches of rain around 7pm. As the picture shows, the sky was clear and the sun was shining.

description:
One large white domestic Mallard ("Pekin Duck") and a slightly smaller-sized normal-plumaged trio.
At the time, I was unable to judge accurately if the ones with typical plumage had the deep belly of domestic Mallard strains but I was not especially familiar with the proportion/structure differences between domestic Mallards and wild Mallards. They seemed to be more or less the same size as the Muscovy Ducks present.

I observed one of the drakes mating with Muscovy ducks during the time I observed the area.

These Mallards looked kind of dumpy and bigger than I would expect wild, migratory Mallards to be. Additionally, all "real" Mallards in Florida are migratory--only spending the Winter months here and they are typically present in Florida only from November to March or April. So these were definitely not migratory birds since June is too late for a nonresident migratory duck to be present.


In any case, feral Mallards in Florida during the Summer/breeding season (such as these) are considered "nuisance Mallards" by wildlife agencies due to their propensity for hybridizing with Florida's Mottled Ducks--potentially leading to the eventual extinction of Mottled Ducks:

description:
With Valeri Ponzo, a successful search for her lifer American Black Ducks -- and the American Flamingo and the 2 Vermilion Flycatchers weren't bad either ... The weather was sunny, cool, and breezy. We parked at the gate along the main refuge road and first enjoyed the male Vermilion Flycatcher for several minutes before we started walking the Stony Bayou dikes. At the fork, we took the left (northern) dike, which passes by a stand of scraggly Slash Pines; there seemed to be more open water visible from this dike than from the southern dike. At 1235, we found 7 Mallards and what appeared to be 2 American Black Ducks foraging in the pool, but the lighting was poor; the sun was nearly overhead and we were looking south. After I returned to our rental truck to get a second spotting scope (Val's Kowa scope is much better but much heavier than my Eagle Optics scope; we kept the Kowa in the truck to avoid carrying it for up to 5 miles unless necessary -- it was now necessary ...), we studied the ducks and identified and counted the ducks and shorebirds as best as possible given the lighting conditions, until about 1420.

We then continued east (then south, then west) to look for the American Flamingo, which was the sole target of nearly every other birder that we encountered along the trail (in fact, most of the others had never even heard of an American Black Duck!). After enjoying the flamingo for more than 20 minutes -- this was, by far, the best look that either of us have had of a (presumed wild) American Flamingo -- we continued west along the dike that forms the southern boundary of Stony Bayou. Within a few hundred feet of the flamingo, we found a female Vermilion Flycatcher that we were unaware of; for a while we thought that we had discovered it ("thanks" to Don Fraser for bursting our bubble via text message) ...

As we approached the original fork, at 1625, we had excellent light to the east, and found the 7 Mallards and the 2 American Black Ducks foraging in apparently the same spot as they had been 2-4 hours earlier. This time the lighting was superb and Val was able to see the diagnostic field marks of the black ducks; the flock was courteous enough to get up and fly around for 30-50 seconds before settling back down. Upon reaching our truck, we again spent several minutes enjoying the male Vermilion Flycatcher before heading home, at 1700.

I checked to see how many observations of Mallards there were for Cross Creek County Park. and didn't find any, so I feel bound to post these photos that are seven and a half years old. 2017 was a year that saw a lot of dead Carp floating in this man-made lake, in fact I cropped one out of these images, just out of frame to the upper right. I have seen a variety of Ducks on this public lake, both of the dabbling and diving sorts. 

This male Mallard has a curiously uneven chestnut coloured chest. I don't know what that signifies, if anything. In the month of May, why would some body feathers be atypical? Age related? Mixed breed genetics? Mallards can be confusing because of partial domestication. This one was definitely hanging out in the wild so to speak, nowhere near where there would be anyone feeding it. These pictures were made with a 250 millimeter lens, and I don't think he was aware of me at all. I was hidden in a pretty dense wood on shore. 

Cross Creek Lake was constructed in 1979 and covers about 244 acres in the rolling hills of the Allegheny Plateau, surrounded by mixed deciduous woodland and small farms. Elevation 313 meters (1027 feet).

For thoughts on the carp I found dead on the same day, see:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/251905986

description: With Valeri Ponzo; a successful search for our year Gadwall. We had never been here before but saw that Gadwall had recently been reported to eBird, so we decided to visit. We stayed 2.5 hours; we had a great morning here, with birds such a Gadwall, Green-winged Teal, Ruddy Duck, Stilt Sandpiper, and American Pipit! It would be fun to try to hit 50 species from this spot -- if the pond remains natural rather than becoming part of The Villages, which threatens to subsume most of the county.. Other than walking 50 feet south of County Road to check out that pond and walking along the fenceline east and west a couple hundred feet to get better photographs, we did not move from where we parked. The weather was clear with a light fog and cool, with calm winds at the start, becoming sunny and warm by the end. We left at 1054 and headed to Dade Battlefield.
